stories.headline: J&K inflation climbs for 5th straight month to 4.27%
stories.title: J&K inflation climbs for 5th straight month to 4.27%
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 18: Retail inflation in Jammu and Kashmir rose for the fifth consecutive month to 4.27 percent in September, with urban consumers facing greater price pressures than their rural counterparts as the cost of food and essential commodities continued to squeeze household budgets. Data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) show that inflation increased from 4.09 percent in August to 4.27 percent in September. Rural inflation stood at 4.12 percent, while the urban rate was higher at 4.65 percent. Inflation has climbed steadily from 2.67 percent in April to 2.84 percent in May, 3.52 percent in June, 3.87 percent in July, 4.09 percent in August and 4.27 percent in September — an increase of 1.60 percentage points since April. Jammu and Kashmir's trend differs from the national pattern, where rural inflation stood at 6.08 percent in September against 4.88 percent in urban areas. In the Union Territory, urban inflation exceeded rural inflation by 0.53 percentage points. Consumers in Srinagar and other urban centres have pointed to rising prices of vegetables, pulses, poultry and other essentials. "The prices of essentials have gone up, and we are hapless," said Jan Mohammed. Javid Ahmad, a Srinagar resident, said rising prices were affecting almost every household. As more income goes towards daily necessities, families have less left for savings and other expenses. Around 60 percent of Jammu and Kashmir's food requirement is met through supplies from outside the Union Territory, according to the figures cited in the analysis. Transportation, handling and distribution costs add to retail prices, while supply disruptions can further increase costs. Pressure on agricultural land and limited local production of some essential food commodities add to this dependence. Although horticulture, particularly apple production, is an important source of income for the region, Jammu and Kashmir continues to rely heavily on outside markets for everyday food supplies. This dependence leaves consumers exposed to price fluctuations in producing states and makes local markets vulnerable to transport bottlenecks and seasonal shortages. Expanding local food production and improving storage and supply-chain infrastructure could help reduce this exposure. Retail inflation across India rose to 5.54 percent in September from 4.83 percent in August, driven largely by food prices. Onion inflation surged to 108.09 percent from 48.78 percent in August, while garlic inflation reached 54.62 percent, according to the figures cited in the analysis. Jammu and Kashmir's September inflation rate remained 1.27 percentage points below the national figure. Between January and September, inflation averaged 2.97 percent in the Union Territory against 4.00 percent nationally. The position contrasts with April-December 2025, when J&K's average inflation stood at 3.60 percent, more than twice the national average of 1.72 percent. The coming months could bring further pressure on household budgets as winter reduces the availability of some locally grown vegetables and increases reliance on supplies from outside the Union Territory. The extent of any additional price rise will depend on local arrivals, transport conditions and prices in supplying markets. The October inflation reading, scheduled for release on November 12, will offer a clearer indication of whether the recent rise is continuing. With inflation increasing for five consecutive months, food prices remain a key concern for households already facing pressure on their disposable incomes.

stories.headline: CJI Surya Kant inaugurates Ladakh Bench of J&K and Ladakh High Court
stories.title: CJI Surya Kant inaugurates Ladakh Bench of J&K and Ladakh High Court
stories.summary: Leh, Oct 18: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant on Sunday inaugurated the newly established Ladakh Bench of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh at Melongthang in Leh, marking a significant milestone in bringing constitutional justice closer to the people of the Union Territory. The new bench is expected to ease the hardships faced by litigants who have long had to travel to Srinagar or Jammu to pursue their cases, often incurring substantial expenses and losing time due to difficult terrain and harsh climatic conditions. Hearing of cases at the Leh bench is scheduled to commence on October 21. The High Court has identified 75 cases for listing before the bench, with a Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Sanjay Parihar set to take up the initial batch. Upon his arrival, the Chief Justice of India was accorded a ceremonial Guard of Honour, following which he unveiled the inauguration plaque and toured the court complex. The formal proceedings began with the National Song and National Anthem, followed by a welcome address by Chief Justice Bhati. The ceremony was attended by Supreme Court Justices M MSundresh, P S Narasimha and ArunPalli; Attorney General for India R Venkataramani; Lieutenant Governor of LadakhVinai Kumar Saxena; Chief Justice Bhati and other judges of the High Court; and Chief Secretary Ladakh Ashish Kumar Kundra. Former Chief Justice of the High Court Justice TashiRabstan, senior judicial officers, representatives of the Bar Associations of Leh and Kargil, and officials of the civil administration, police and other departments were also present. Addressing the gathering, Justice Surya Kant said the significance of the new bench lay not merely in its location at an altitude of around 3,500 metres but in its proximity to the people it serves. “Access to justice, after all, begins not in the Court's compound, but at the litigant's door,” he said. The CJI emphasised the role of technology, legal aid and e-SewaKendras in ensuring that people in remote areas could access judicial services without geographical barriers. He announced that the Supreme Court would list matters originating from Ladakh on a single day once adequate video-conferencing facilities were available to lawyers practising before the new bench. The apex court would also hear such matters through video conferencing on a day-to-day basis, enabling lawyers from Leh and Kargil to argue cases without travelling to New Delhi. The arrangement, he said, would reduce the time and expense involved in pursuing cases before the country's highest court. Digital initiatives and green infrastructure A major highlight of the inauguration was the launch of digital and infrastructure initiatives intended to modernise judicial functioning and improve access to justice. The CJI launched the e-Filing Portal and Document Management System (DMS) for the Ladakh Bench, along with the High Court's Online Recruitment Portal. The e-Filing Portal will enable advocates and litigants, particularly those living in remote areas, to file cases electronically without travelling to the court. The DMS will facilitate digital management of judicial records, while the recruitment portal is intended to promote transparency, accessibility and efficiency in recruitment for the High Court and district judiciary. The Ladakh Bench will function as a fully IT-enabled, paperless court. The court complex houses a digitisationcentre, filing counter, bar room, litigants' sitting area, conference room and video-conferencing room. The CJI also virtually inaugurated the Green Wall initiative, symbolising the judiciary's commitment to environmental conservation and ecological sustainability in Ladakh. The initiative was marked by the presentation of planters to dignitaries and the screening of a short video. Justice Surya Kant also initiated work for the installation of solar power systems at 11 locations, reinforcing the judiciary's focus on renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure. In his special address, Lieutenant Governor Saxena welcomed the establishment of the bench and highlighted the importance of the Green Wall initiative in protecting Ladakh's fragile environment. He described the new bench as a “historic milestone” and a new era of accessible justice. In a post on X, Saxena said the initiative would fulfil a long-standing demand of the people by reducing distant travel and financial burdens while strengthening the judicial system in the Union Territory. He also expressed gratitude to Prime Minister NarendraModi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah for their support in advancing institutional development and inclusive growth in Ladakh. The establishment of the bench was approved by the Union Government in August, after which the High Court designated Leh as the sitting venue on October 5. Judicial leaders underline access to justice In his welcome address, Chief Justice Bhati said access to justice had been the guiding principle behind the establishment of the Ladakh Bench. He described the creation of a constitutional court in one of the world's highest-altitude regions as a significant step towards ensuring judicial access for people living in geographically challenging areas. Supreme Court Justices M MSundresh, P S Narasimha and ArunPalli, along with Attorney General R Venkataramani, also addressed the gathering. The programme concluded with a vote of thanks by Chief Secretary Ashish Kumar Kundra, followed by the National Song and National Anthem. Separately, a ceremonial bench of the High Court was held in Leh under the chairmanship of Chief Justice Bhati to commemorate the inauguration. Thirteen other High Court judges participated in the proceedings, reflecting the significance attached to the establishment of the new bench. Addressing the ceremonial sitting, Deputy Solicitor General of India for the Jammu Wing Vishal Sharma described the bench as a reaffirmation of the constitutional promise of accessible justice, strengthening the rule of law and bringing constitutional remedies closer to the people. Deputy Solicitor General of India for the Srinagar Wing Tahir Majid Shamsi traced the evolution of judicial institutions in Ladakh since 2019. He said regular judicial sittings, digital facilities and legal aid would substantially alleviate the difficulties faced by litigants. Advocate GonboStobgyal, president of the Bar Association, Leh, described the inauguration as the fulfilment of a long-cherished aspiration of the people and assured the judiciary of the Bar's cooperation in the effective administration of justice. Advocate Reyaz Ahmad Khan, president of the Bar Association, Kargil, also termed the establishment of the bench a historic milestone and acknowledged the sustained efforts of the judicial leadership in bringing justice closer to the region. Chief Justice Bhati said the people of Ladakh had endured difficult terrain, harsh weather and substantial travel expenses to pursue cases in Srinagar and Jammu. The permanent bench, he said, would help ensure that geographical isolation did not translate into judicial exclusion. He expressed gratitude to the CJI, the Union Government, the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Ladakh administration for their collective efforts in translating the initiative into reality. Bhati also urged the Bench and the Bar to uphold constitutional values, safeguard the rights of vulnerable sections and protect Ladakh's fragile environment, envisioning the new institution as a source of fairness and timely justice for generations to come. A significant development during the ceremonial proceedings was the adoption of a Full Court resolution calling for improved access to education and safe, accessible and affordable residential facilities for girl students in Ladakh, particularly those from remote and far-flung areas. Recognising the challenges posed by geographical isolation, long travel distances and inadequate accommodation, the resolution called for greater legal awareness and coordinated efforts involving educational institutions, legal services authorities and other stakeholders to ensure equal educational opportunities. The Full Court requested the Regular Bench to take further action on the matter. The inauguration of the Ladakh Bench, alongside the introduction of digital facilities and sustainable infrastructure initiatives, is expected to strengthen local judicial services, reduce the burden on litigants and improve access to constitutional remedies across the Union Territory.

stories.headline: Power cuts return to haunt Kashmir
stories.title: Power cuts return to haunt Kashmir
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 18: As temperatures begin to dip across Kashmir, power cuts have returned to haunt consumers, reviving questions about the government’s ability to ensure a reliable electricity supply during winter despite promises of improvement and higher power tariffs. The Kashmir Power Distribution Corporation Limited (KPDCL), under its revised curtailment schedule effective October 17, has prescribed up to eight hours of daily power cuts in several areas, while other feeders face six or three hours of scheduled outages. Essential feeders have been exempted, and feeders declared to receive round-the-clock power and low-loss feeders have generally been assigned 30 minutes of curtailment in a single daytime slot. Under the revised schedule, several areas across Kashmir will face eight hours of daily power curtailment, while others have been allocated six or three hours of cuts. Feeders with AT&C losses exceeding 65 percent have been assigned eight hours of daily curtailment, those with losses between 40.5 and 65 percent face six hours, and feeders with losses between 15 and 40.5 percent have been allotted three hours. Essential feeders have been exempted from scheduled curtailment, while feeders declared to receive round-the-clock power and low-loss feeders have generally been assigned 30 minutes of curtailment in a single daytime slot. The curtailments come less than two months after a revised electricity tariff structure took effect on September 1, with the Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC) approving an average tariff increase of 6.83 per cent for the period up to March 31, 2027. The increase has put the National Conference government under pressure to deliver on its electoral assurances on electricity supply, as consumers face higher tariffs while continuing to deal with scheduled outages. The immediate trigger is the seasonal rise in electricity demand as households increasingly depend on power for heating, lighting and other essential needs. But the recurring winter curtailments also point to deeper structural challenges: limited growth in locally controlled generation capacity, dependence on electricity purchased from outside, high distribution losses and the unfinished task of modernising the power distribution network. Electricity demand in Jammu and Kashmir rises substantially during winter, when heating requirements increase and hydropower generation can be affected by seasonal variations in water availability. The latest curtailment schedule does not specify the current peak demand, the power available to KPDCL or the size of any deficit. Nevertheless, the allocation of several hours of scheduled curtailment to individual feeders indicates the pressure on the distribution system as winter approaches. The challenge is particularly significant because electricity demand is not limited to households. Shops, workshops, hotels, restaurants, small manufacturing units and other commercial establishments depend on a reasonably uninterrupted supply to operate equipment, preserve goods, serve customers and maintain business hours. For businesses already dealing with seasonal fluctuations, prolonged power cuts can mean lost working hours, lower productivity and additional expenditure on backup arrangements. Small establishments that cannot afford generators or other alternatives are particularly vulnerable. One of the central weaknesses in Jammu and Kashmir’s power sector is the gap between growing consumption and the limited expansion of generation capacity directly reflected in the Union Territory’s own installed-capacity figures. The Digest of Statistics 2024-25 published by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics shows that installed power capacity stood at 1,372.40 MW from 2019-20 through 2024-25, after being recorded at 1414.17 MW in 2018-19. The figures indicate that the reported installed capacity remained broadly unchanged over six consecutive years. This is an important distinction: Jammu and Kashmir has substantial hydropower potential, and several major projects have been under development. However, planned capacity and projects under construction cannot meet consumers’ needs until they are commissioned and begin supplying electricity. The Union Territory has therefore continued to rely heavily on power purchased from central generating stations and other sources to meet its requirements, particularly during winter. The dependence on purchased electricity leaves the local distribution system exposed to the cost and availability of power procured from outside. It also makes timely commissioning of new generation projects and improvements in the use of existing resources important components of any long-term strategy to reduce winter shortages. However, the installed-capacity figures alone do not establish that actual generation has declined or remained unchanged in every year. Hydropower output fluctuates with water availability, and a precise assessment of the contribution of local generation to the current shortage would require updated generation, purchase and demand figures. The other major challenge is the amount of electricity lost before it is billed and revenue is collected. Jammu and Kashmir continues to record high aggregate technical and commercial losses, particularly in the Kashmir distribution system. According to figures reported in July 2026, Jammu and Kashmir recorded AT&C losses of 33.54 percent in 2024-25, compared with the national average of 15.04 percent. The figures placed the Union Territory among the worst-performing power distribution systems in the country.

stories.headline: Russia sanctions waiver is a 60-day pause; Europe refused to target India, China over oil: US
stories.title: Russia sanctions waiver is a 60-day pause; Europe refused to target India, China over oil: US
stories.summary: The decision has triggered political opposition in Washington, with lawmakers questioning its implications for Ukraine and the enforcement of sanctions against Moscow.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amid intense criticism, the US on Sunday said the waiver of sanctions on Russia and tariffs on other countries, including India, was a 60-day pause to analyse the global impact of the measure.
Trump’s cabinet colleagues Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent said the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act granted the President the flexibility to assess the situation.

“No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” Bessent told NBC’s Meet the Press, referring to the Executive Order signed by Trump granting a waiver from sanctions under the Graham Act passed with overwhelming bipartisan support last month.
Bessent revealed that the US had asked its European allies to impose secondary sanctions on China and India for buying Russian oil, but they refused.
“So why should the US bear the burden?
President Trump, perhaps we will be in contact with our European partners.
Why should the US go it alone,” Bessent said, adding that European countries had waived an embargo on purchase of Russian diesel and jet fuel in May.

On Saturday evening, Secretary of State Rubio said waivers were included in the Graham Act to study the different things going around the world, such as the pressure on global energy supplies due to the Iran war, the attack of Houthis in Saudi Arabia and the Ukraine-Russia war.

“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters before leaving on a six-day visit to Uzbekistan and India.

The executive order signed by Trump on Friday states that the waivers shall remain in effect until such time as the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury and the Trade Representative, as appropriate, determine that further action is appropriate.
Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago resort near Miami on Saturday, Trump said his decision to waive sanctions under the Graham Act would benefit the US.
“A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said.

body: “No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” Bessent told NBC’s Meet the Press, referring to the Executive Order signed by Trump granting a waiver from sanctions under the Graham Act passed with overwhelming bipartisan support last month.
Bessent revealed that the US had asked its European allies to impose secondary sanctions on China and India for buying Russian oil, but they refused.
“So why should the US bear the burden?
President Trump, perhaps we will be in contact with our European partners.
Why should the US go it alone,” Bessent said, adding that European countries had waived an embargo on purchase of Russian diesel and jet fuel in May.

On Saturday evening, Secretary of State Rubio said waivers were included in the Graham Act to study the different things going around the world, such as the pressure on global energy supplies due to the Iran war, the attack of Houthis in Saudi Arabia and the Ukraine-Russia war.

“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters before leaving on a six-day visit to Uzbekistan and India.

The executive order signed by Trump on Friday states that the waivers shall remain in effect until such time as the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury and the Trade Representative, as appropriate, determine that further action is appropriate.

stories.headline: Kashmir University orders stock verification of library books
stories.title: Kashmir University orders stock verification of library books
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 18: Authorities at Kashmir University (KU) have directed all departments, research centres, campuses and directorates to undertake physical verification of library books and submit verified reports within two months. As per the fresh circular instructions, the departments and research centres have been asked to focus on scrutiny of missing books and losses involving high-value titles. The circular instructions in this regard have been issued by Librarian of the Allama Iqbal Library of the varsity on October 16, 2026. The KU Librarian has asked Heads of Departments (HoDs) and Directors of various research centres, directorates and campuses to immediately initiate the stock-verification exercise to ensure accountability, proper maintenance and accurate updating of library assets. The concerned departments and centres have been asked to constitute internal stock-verification committees and submit final reports along with the prescribed annexures to the University Librarian's office within the stipulated period. The exercise will cover total library holdings, books currently available, weeded-out titles, books damaged in the 2014 floods, losses reported by users, books in circulation and records of books issued or consulted between January 2001 and December 2025. The University has also directed departments to calculate missing-book losses in accordance with the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, particularly Rule 215, read with the University Library Committee's resolutions. Under the prescribed procedure, institutions will have to reconcile missing-book figures with circulation records to establish whether the losses fall within the permissible limits. As per the circular instructions, the HoDs and Directors have been asked to submit detailed written explanations in cases where a missing book has a purchase cost exceeding Rs 1,000. The instructions have been issued along with the amendments to the University's stock-verification regulations approved by the Library Committee, which provide that the loss of five books per 1,000 volumes issued or consulted annually may be considered reasonable, provided the losses are not attributable to dishonesty or negligence. The amended provision, according to the committee's minutes dated January 23, 2025, is to be applied retrospectively. The committee has also clarified that books consulted within library premises for reading, reference or study, as well as those taken off shelves for photocopying without formal issuance, will be counted as consulted books while calculating allowable losses. For the purpose of estimating consultations, the committee has prescribed figures of three books for students, five each for scholars and faculty members, and one book for staff and other officials. The University has prescribed separate formats for stock verification and the preparation of missing-book lists. In view of this, all the departments will have to provide details such as accession numbers, titles, authors and printed prices of missing books, with the total cost to be calculated by Allama Iqbal Library. "The missing-book lists must be prepared in MS Excel and sent through the official email ID of the concerned Head of Department to the designated library email addresses," the circular reads.
